parts: Your hallway light is counting down, and you cannot see it.
You press a button. The light comes on. You climb the stairs, and halfway up, click. Darkness.
That is not a glitch. It is a staircase timer, doing exactly what it was built to do.
So why do hallway lights turn themselves off?
A staircase timer is a timed switch for stairs, corridors, or building lobbies.
One press turns the light on. After a set time, it switches off by itself.
According to Wikipedia, the light stays on for long enough to go up or down the stairs.
In a single home, the stair light usually stays on until someone switches it off.
A shared building is different. Wikipedia says the landlord usually pays for the shared lighting, and tenants have little reason to switch it off.
Here is our reading. When a light belongs to everyone, nobody feels it is their job to turn it off. A timer takes over that job.
Wikipedia also says time switches can save energy, because equipment runs only when it is needed.
Wikipedia says the first units were pneumatic push-button timers, known as dashpot timers.
A big button pushes in a spring-loaded piston, and that holds the contacts closed.
A pneumatic dashpot slows the piston on its way back. That slow return is the delay.
There are also electronic timers, with no moving parts.
With an electronic timer, Wikipedia says any number of buttons can trigger it. One timer, many buttons.
Wikipedia says pressing again extends the light, because the delay counts from your last press.
One manufacturer lists a delay you can adjust from half a minute to twelve minutes.
Its page also lists a switch-off pre-warning, a signal before the light goes out.
There is also a mode for continuous light. Some systems use a key switch for that, for example for cleaning.
The idea is old. A French patent record published in nineteen twenty-nine carries a title that translates as time switch for staircase lighting.
Today, Wikipedia says a motion sensor can replace the button.
A timer is still needed. Wikipedia says sensors are not perfectly reliable, and without a timer the lights could flash off and on.
So when the hall light goes off by itself, it is most likely not broken. The countdown simply ended.
Here is our reading. It is a tiny rule built into the wall: the light stays just long enough, then steps aside.
Many buildings hide other quiet machines. Somewhere in there, another small box counts something you cannot see. Its numbers climb, and nobody presses a button.
